title: Agent Marketplace
content: Agent Marketplace The agent marketplace is a catalog of community-built agents hosted on GitHub. Agav reads the catalog at startup (when you open the Marketplace tab) and lets you install agents directly into your global or project configuration. Opening the marketplace The marketplace tab fetches from the configured marketplace URL and displays all available agents. Browsing agents Agents are displayed three per page. Navigate with: | Key | Action | | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | | / | Move selection within the current page | | / | Previous / next page | | | Open search — filter by name, description, category, or tag | | | Inspect selected agent (shows tools, credentials, and description) | | | Refresh from the marketplace URL | | | Update the selected agent to the latest marketplace version | | | Clear search / exit | Agents already installed on your system show a or badge. Installing an agent Select an agent and press . If the agent is not yet installed, a destination prompt appears: Press or to install. If the agent is already installed at project scope, pressing offers to promote it to global (removes the project copy and reinstalls globally). Globally installed agents block re-installation at project scope — use the List tab to manage them instead. Configuring after install After installing, switch to the List tab to configure credentials: The config editor shows each required credential with its current status ( or ). Press on a field to edit it, paste your value, and press again to save. Values are encrypted at rest. CLI installation Install without opening the TUI: Remote installs are restricted to trusted git hosts: github.com, gitlab.com, bitbucket.org, and raw.githubusercontent.com. Set (comma-separated) to allow additional hosts. Agent names must start with a letter or digit and contain only lowercase letters, digits, dots, hyphens, or underscores (max 64 characters). Local marketplace For local development and testing, clone the marketplace repo and set: The environment variable overrides the config file value and the built-in default. Hosting a marketplace Any GitHub repository (or static file server) can act as a marketplace. The minimum structure: See the official marketplace repository for a complete example. Deleting agents When a globally installed, user-created agent (one without a marketplace ) is deleted from the List or Create tab, Agav automatically saves it as a template before removal. Project-scoped user-created agents are deleted without a template. The template preserves the agent's name, description, system prompt, MCP server selections, and tags. You can restore it later from the Create tab (). Marketplace agents (those installed from a URL) are deleted without creating a template — they can be reinstalled from the marketplace at any time. title: Agents
content: Agents Agents are named, purpose-built sub-agents that extend Agav with domain-specific capabilities. Each agent has its own tool set, system prompt, and isolated credentials. When your query involves a task an agent handles — listing GitHub PRs, searching Jira tickets, taking a screenshot — the LLM routes to it automatically. How agents work When Agav starts, it loads all enabled agents and registers each one as a callable tool. The LLM reads a compact catalog (one line per agent, capped at ~500 tokens total) and chooses the right agent for the task. An agent invocation runs a nested agent loop with the agent's tools, system prompt, and credentials — fully isolated from the parent session. Results stream back to you normally. Loading order Agav discovers agents from three locations. Later tiers override earlier ones by name, so you can replace a bundled agent with a custom version: | Tier | Location | Override priority | | --- | --- | --- | | Bundled | Shipped with Agav binary (currently empty — reserved for future built-in agents) | Lowest | | Global | | Middle | | Project | in the working directory | Highest | Installing agents from the marketplace Browse and install agents from the community marketplace: See Agent Marketplace for full details. Creating agents You can create custom agents directly from the TUI without writing a manifest by hand: The Create tab opens a "My Agents" hub that lists your user-created agents and any saved templates. From here you can create a new agent or restore one from a template. Wizard flow Selecting New Agent launches a five-step wizard: 1. Name & Description — pick a unique agent name and a short description of what it does. 2. System Prompt — write the agent's system prompt, or press to auto-generate one. The LLM uses your name and description to draft a prompt you can edit before continuing. 3. Native Tools — select the built-in Agav tools the agent can use. This creates the manifest's allowlist; leave every option unchecked if the agent should use only its local and MCP tools. 4. MCP Servers — select which MCP servers the agent should have access to. The list is populated from your workspace config ( in or ). 5. Review & Save — preview the full agent definition and confirm. The agent is saved to and immediately available for use. Templates When you delete a user-created agent, Agav automatically saves it as a template so you can recreate it later without starting from scratch. - Templates appear in the Create tab's "My Agents" list with a label. - Opening a template pre-populates the wizard with the original name, description, system prompt, and MCP server selections — edit anything before saving. - Press on a template in the list to remove it permanently. - Templates are stored in . Per-agent MCP servers Agents can declare MCP servers in their manifest. Each server entry supports an field for passing environment variables (API keys, base URLs, etc.) to the server process. Servers are started when the agent runs and stopped when it finishes — they are fully scoped to the agent's lifecycle and do not affect the parent session or other agents. Credentials Each agent declares the environment variables it needs ( in the manifest). Credentials are: - Stored encrypted in — never in plain text - Injected into only during that agent's execution — not shared with other agents or the parent session - Editable from the agent inspect view: Agents with missing credentials show a indicator in the List tab. The LLM receives an error message if it tries to call an unconfigured agent. Tool permissions and confirmation Every tool in an agent is classified as either (read-only) or (creates, edits, or deletes data): - Safe tools run without a confirmation prompt. - Destructive tools pause and display a confirmation before executing. The classification is declared in the agent manifest () and is visible in the inspect view. Native tool access Native agents do not automatically receive Agav's built-in tools. Select the tools they need during creation, or open and edit Native Tools. The chosen tools are written to the agent's manifest allowlist. Leaving the list empty keeps built-in tools unavailable while preserving agent-local and declared MCP tools. Bundled and A2A agents cannot edit this setting. Agent sandbox Non-bundled agent tools run inside an OS-level sandbox that is stricter than the shell sandbox used by : | Property | Agent sandbox | Shell sandbox | | --- | --- | --- | | Default policy | Deny all, then allow specific paths | Allow all, then deny specific paths | | Network | Denied | Allowed | | Filesystem writes | Working directory and temp directory only | Allowed except system directories | | Credential directories | , , denied | Same | | Environment secrets | Stripped (, , , , …) | Stripped | On macOS the agent sandbox uses a deny-default Seatbelt profile; on Linux it uses Bubblewrap with . Bundled agent tools are excluded from sandboxing since they ship with Agav. Model and effort overrides Agents inherit the session's model and effort by default. You can override them per-agent in the config editor (). The override is stored in the agent's and shown as in the inspect view. Clear the value to revert to inheriting from the session. CLI TUI Open to manage agents interactively. The three tabs are: - * — view, inspect, enable/disable, and remove installed agents. - — browse and install community agents. - * — create new agents with the wizard, and manage your agents and templates. Related - Agent Marketplace — browse and install community agents - Agent Manifest reference — full AGENT.md format - Build a Native Agent — write your own agent - Install and Configure an Agent — step-by-step walkthrough - Build an Agent from a Template — restore and customize a saved template

title: Background Processes
content: Background Processes Agav's tool manages long-running shell commands without blocking the main agent turn. Use it for dev servers, slow integration tests, builds, local scripts, and other trusted commands that should keep running after the current Agav UI exits. For repeated agent prompts, use or . For repeated shell commands that should become daemon-backed jobs, use , , or . Purpose Background processes solve two common automation problems: - Non-blocking long commands — start a shell command and keep chatting while it runs. - Durable command jobs — persist job state and logs so a command can complete after Agav exits and be reported when Agav starts again. Architecture - writes a job record, generates if needed, and launches a detached Node runner. - The runner executes the command with in the selected working directory, captures stdout and stderr, and updates the persisted job record. - Job status moves through and , then one terminal state: , , , or . - Jobs continue running after Agav exits because the runner is detached from the interactive UI. - When Agav starts again, the interactive UI scans persisted records every 2 seconds while a session is open. - Completed jobs that have not been reported yet are added to the main chat once with the command and last output, then marked with so they are not reported repeatedly on later restarts. - Process IDs are 8-character IDs. , , , and accept a full ID or a prefix; use a unique prefix to avoid matching the wrong record. Storage and reattach By default, records and logs live under the Agav config directory at : The job JSON record contains: Set before starting Agav to store records and logs somewhere else, for example during tests: When Agav restarts, it reads persisted records from the same directory. If a completed record has no , the UI reports it once and updates the record. Relative paths are resolved before launch. | | | optional for , | | Number of stdout/stderr log lines to return. Maximum: . | | | optional for | | Maximum time to wait before returning. Maximum: . | | | optional for | | Signal sent to the child PID and runner PID when reachable. | The output is plain text in Agav's standard tool result shape: Actions | Action | Behavior | | --- | --- | | | Starts a detached daemon-backed command and returns the process ID. The command is blocked if it matches Agav's destructive-command blocklist. | | | Lists all persisted background process records from the active background-process directory. | | | Returns one process record with status, PID when known, duration, cwd, and command. | | | Returns process metadata plus captured stdout and stderr tails. | | | Polls until the process reaches a terminal state or expires, then returns logs. If the timeout expires first, it reports that the job is still running. | | | Marks the process as killed and sends to the child PID and runner PID when reachable. | Status values shown in , , , and are formatted as , , , , , or . Usage examples Ask Agav to use the background process tool when a command should not block the main turn: Then ask for updates by ID: Typical returned status text looks like: When the job finishes, Agav adds a system message to the main chat: Failed and killed jobs are also reported once. If stderr has output, the notification's uses stderr before stdout. Scheduled background commands Use to save a recurring shell command that starts a daemon-backed process directly, without an LLM turn at trigger time: Aliases are equivalent: Manage process schedules with the same commands as prompt schedules: marks background-command entries as and shows . Prompt schedules remain entries and are created with . The distinction matters at trigger time: - submits the saved prompt to the agent as an automated turn. - , , and start the saved command directly with the tool and do not wait for an LLM turn. Schedules are stored in . Agav must be running in the interactive UI when the cron expression matches; the scheduler checks once every 30 seconds and runs matching tasks at most once per minute. Once a process schedule starts its daemon job, that job continues after Agav exits and is reported on the next running session when it completes. Configuration | Setting or variable | Default | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | Background process directory | | Holds process records, captured logs, and the generated runner script. Override with . | | | default directory when unset | Absolute or relative directory used instead of for all background process records and logs. Useful for tests or relocating job state. Use the same value across restarts to reattach to those jobs. | | Runner executable | | Node executable used to launch . Override with . | | | unset | Node.js executable used by daemon runners when the current runtime cannot execute the generated runner script. | | Wait timeout | ms | Per-call default for ; capped at ms. | | Log tail | lines | Per-call default for and ; capped at lines. | Set before starting Agav when packaged or custom runtimes need a specific Node.js binary for daemon jobs: For isolated manual tests, combine both environment variables: Safety and permissions - , , , and are treated as safe tool calls. - and are sensitive process-control actions. In mode, they require confirmation unless an rule applies. - The confirmation prompt for explicitly warns that the command starts a daemon-backed background process that can keep running after Agav exits and may write files, use network, and consume CPU, memory, or disk. - The confirmation prompt for explicitly warns that the signal can stop work currently in progress. - In mode or headless mode without a confirmation handler, and are blocked unless the call is otherwise safe or explicitly allowed by the current policy. - skips normal confirmation prompts. Use narrow patterns such as instead of allowing every call. - A bare allowlist rule permits every process action. Scoped rules match the command for , the ID for , and the ID/action for read-only process calls. - Commands that match Agav's destructive-command blocklist, such as , are blocked by the process tool before they start. - , , and are explicit slash commands. Creating the schedule is treated as user consent for that command. At trigger time they start the configured command directly, without an LLM turn or confirmation prompt. Schedule only trusted, non-interactive commands. - Background process commands are launched by the daemon runner rather than through the normal timeout and sandbox path. Run only commands you trust, avoid interactive commands, and quote shell input carefully. - Environment variables whose names look like credentials (, , , , , or ) are stripped before spawning the runner and child command. Troubleshooting A job stays in The detached runner may not have started. If you are using a packaged runtime or custom launcher, set to a known Node.js executable and start Agav again: Then start a new background process and inspect it with or . Completion was not reported Completion notifications are emitted by the interactive UI. If Agav was closed when the job finished, restart Agav with the same value, then wait a few seconds. A completed job with in its JSON record has already been reported. Logs are missing Use first. If no output is shown, inspect the job's stdout and stderr files under the active background-process directory. Commands that buffer output may not write lines until they exit. A scheduled background command did not run Agav must be open when the cron expression matches. Run and confirm the task is enabled and marked . Prompt schedules are marked and submit text to the agent instead of starting a command directly. Manual test checklist For release testing, use the full Background Process Manual Test Plan in a disposable repository. At minimum, verify: 1. Start a background command that prints a known string after a short delay; confirm the UI remains usable and a completion notification appears. 2. Run list, poll, log, and wait requests against the process ID; confirm logs include the known output. 3. Start a longer job, exit Agav, wait for completion, then restart Agav; confirm the reattach notification appears once and is not repeated on another restart. 4. Add , , or for the next minute; confirm shows , the command starts without an LLM turn, and completion is reported. 5. Confirm an existing prompt task still appears as and submits to the agent at its scheduled time. 6. Start a long process, kill it, then poll it; confirm the status is or the selected signal. 7. Confirm a destructive command such as is refused by the process tool. 8. If testing a packaged runtime, set to a known Node.js executable and repeat the start/log flow. 9. If testing custom storage, set and confirm records, logs, and reattach all use that directory. Clean up stale completed records and logs from or the directory named by when testing is complete. Do not delete active jobs unless they are known test processes.

title: Built-in Tools
content: Built-in Tools Agav exposes these tools to its agent loop. | Tool | Purpose | | --- | --- | | | Read text ranges and preview images, PDFs, and Office documents | | | Create or replace a file | | | Replace one exact, unique string in a file | | | Find names and glob matches | | | Search file contents with regular expressions | | | List a directory | | | Map a repository's directory and symbol structure | | | Execute a shell command with sandbox detection | | | Start, list, poll, log, wait for, and kill daemon-backed background commands | | | Detect and run a supported project test framework | | | Request definitions, references, or hover data from a language server; diagnostic notifications are not yet fully surfaced | | | Read Jupyter notebook cells | | | Change a notebook cell or its type | | | Search the web with DuckDuckGo | | | Send an HTTP request and return the response | | | Create or view GitHub pull requests and issues | | | Update the active plan's current step | | | Persist durable project or user context | | | Delegate an independent task | | | Run a registered skill by name | Connected MCP servers, installed plugins, and active skills can add more tools. Output limits and recovery Tool text returned through Agav's registry is limited to 40,000 UTF-8 bytes and 2,000 lines, including truncation notices. This also covers registered MCP, plugin, skill, and subagent results, errors, and text appended by hooks. Small results are unchanged. Oversized results normally keep a head/tail excerpt with an explicit omission notice; image blocks, error status, and structured result metadata are preserved. Text limits do not cap image token usage. These are fixed implementation limits, not provider-token counts. There is no parameter on , , or , and no configuration setting to raise these limits. Narrow the query or retrieve a specific saved section instead. Saved output paths and retention When output is saved, the notice gives the actual absolute path. The layout is: Agav writes first and publishes by atomic rename. On Unix, directories use mode and files use . Logs can contain private command output or API response data; private permissions are not encryption. - Each saved file holds at most 16 MiB. A partial-log notice means only a prefix was saved, not all omitted content. - Each Agav process has a 128 MiB retention budget, including reservations for unfinished writes, and at most 4,096 capture admissions. Shell and HTTP captures reserve 16 MiB each while pending; publication releases unused reserved bytes. - The per-user temporary root admits 32 process slots, reserving up to 4 GiB of payload capacity across processes sharing that root (plus metadata). - Published logs are not evicted during a live process. Orderly process exit attempts to delete that process's slot, so these paths are not durable session-history attachments. Copy any log you need before exiting Agav. - After a crash, a later startup or first capture can prune a slot only when its recorded creation time is at least 24 hours old and its owner PID is confirmed dead. This is an opportunistic sweep, not a timer or guaranteed 24-hour deletion. Live or reused PIDs, denied probes, unsafe paths, and unknown ownership metadata are conservatively left alone. If storage is full, unavailable, unsafe, or over quota, Agav returns a bounded warning rather than advertising a nonexistent log. Saving failure does not change the original tool's success/error status or rerun its side effects; omitted content may be unavailable. Use the path in the notice with and /, or with a targeted pattern. Recovery calls are bounded too. If uses its JavaScript fallback (always used on Windows), it skips files larger than 1 MiB; use line-range reads or a targeted shell search for larger logs. A saved “complete returned text” file contains what the tool returned, not data the tool already excluded or summarized. In particular, the test runner's raw diagnostic excerpt is not a complete test-process transcript. File reads and repository maps can be absolute or relative to the working directory. Text ranges use 1-based, inclusive and . If only is provided, reading starts at line 1; if only is provided, reading continues toward EOF until the output limit. Ends beyond EOF are clamped, while a start beyond EOF is an error. Invalid or reversed ranges are rejected. Large text files are streamed rather than loaded in full. A bounded text read returns a contiguous prefix of the requested range, reserving room for headers and recovery instructions (at most 1,995 selected whole lines). Its continuation notice identifies the next in the original file, preserving any requested ; no duplicate temporary copy is needed. Follow that notice rather than treating the returned excerpt as the whole file. If the first requested line alone is too long, Agav returns a bounded excerpt and recommends targeted byte extraction with ; repeating that same line range will not advance through the line. PDF and Office ranges use 1-based, inclusive and , with at most 10 pages per preview. Images do not accept line or page ranges, and PDF/Office documents do not accept line ranges. Office fallback behavior depends on available conversion tools: without LibreOffice, uses extracted slide text, while uses extracted text without preserving page ranges or visual layout. See files and context for attachment and preview requirements; attachment limits are separate from these tool-result limits. returns a source-file and symbol skeleton, not file contents or a complete inventory of every file type. Use a project-relative to focus on a subdirectory. counts subdirectories relative to that path: | | Included source files | | --- | --- | | | Files directly in the requested directory only | | | Those files plus files in immediate subdirectories | | or higher | Files through that many subdirectory levels | | Omitted | Unrestricted depth, still subject to the file cap | Depth must be a non-negative safe integer; invalid values fail before traversal. Hidden directories and common dependency, build, cache, and worktree directories are skipped. The map stops at 200 source files and reports that it may be incomplete whenever the cap is reached, even if exactly 200 files exist. Narrow or rather than assuming the first map covered the whole repository. Explicit shallow requests avoid reading deeper source files as well as returning their symbols. Structured test runs and verification supports , , , , and . It detects the framework from the working directory, or accepts a override. selects a test target, not a new working directory; Cargo treats it as a test-name filter. If detection fails, specify the framework or use for the project's own test script. The test process has a 120-second timeout and a 1 MiB output-buffer limit, separate from 's streaming capture. Results show framework and actual test pass/fail counts, up to ten highlighted failures, and short traceback excerpts. Failed or inconclusive runs also show the last 2,000 characters of raw output, plus any process error; this is not a full log. Agav attaches structured verification metadata with , , , , and : | Status | Meaning | | --- | --- | | | Normal zero exit, positive recognized passing-test count, and no recognized failures/errors | | | Nonzero exit, spawn/startup error, timeout/signal, or recognized test failures/errors — even if some tests passed | | | Zero exit but no recognized passing tests (for example, zero tests, skipped-only tests, or unrecognized output) | is null when the process did not exit normally. JavaScript counts come from test summaries rather than suite/file counts; pytest counts come from its result summary rather than warning text; Cargo counts include all recognized suite summaries. An inconclusive result can be non-error, but it is not evidence of successful verification. Merely returning text such as “Passed: 10” without structured metadata is not enough either. A passing in a later tool batch than a successful or counts toward Agav's post-edit verification guard, avoiding redundant “you did not verify” requests. New successful edits invalidate earlier evidence. An edit and check in the same parallel batch do not establish post-edit verification, regardless of result order. Failure wins when multiple checks share a batch; a later passing batch can reverify. Existing shell-check recognition, permissions, hooks, and capped test-repair prompts remain in place; failed edit calls alone do not count as successful modifications, and hook output does not verify an edit. Passing tests do not replace a task-required build, manual run, broader regression checks, warning review, or comparison against expected output. When output is truncated, retrieve the relevant saved sections or use a focused diagnostic command before concluding that warnings and errors are resolved. Context and cost Bounded outputs and focused reads reduce oversized text sent back to the model, but recovery calls add context and may require further model requests. Agav's base instructions also consolidate repeated verification guidance without relaxing the requirements to test after edits, check regressions, build/run/check output, and investigate every warning. These changes do not alter model or effort defaults, remove tools, or change compaction behavior. Byte reductions and avoided redundant verification rounds are not guaranteed billing or throughput savings: tokenization, prompt caching, task scope, and follow-up retrieval all affect the result. Language-server navigation The tool can find definitions, references, and hover information in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, and Go projects when the matching language-server executable is available. | Language | Executable | | --- | --- | | TypeScript or JavaScript | | | Python | | | Rust | | | Go | | Ask Agav for semantic evidence explicitly when a text search is not enough: Agav combines language-server results with file reads and repository search. If the server is unavailable, confirm that its executable is on in the shell that started Agav. Diagnostic notifications are not yet fully surfaced, so use the project's normal diagnostic command when complete output matters. Background processes The tool manages long-running shell commands without blocking the main agent turn. Supported actions are , , , , , and . Background process records and captured logs live under the Agav config directory at by default: Jobs continue after Agav exits. The next interactive session reattaches to persisted records in the active background-process directory and reports completed jobs once in the main chat window. Use to relocate job records and logs, and use to point daemon runners at a specific Node executable when the current runtime cannot run the generated runner script. For recurring shell commands, , , and create process schedules that start daemon-backed jobs directly. remains the prompt-schedule command and submits text to the agent. Read Background Processes for action fields, schedule syntax, persistence details, and safety notes. Confirmations and undo Writes, edits, and sensitive commands can display a confirmation prompt. Edit confirmations include a diff. Choosing the session-wide approval option releases queued confirmations as well. Agav records prior content for tracked file edits in an in-memory undo stack: The stack contains up to twenty changes and does not survive process exit. A newly created file has no previous content to restore. File boundaries The file tools (, , ) enforce path boundary checks. Writes are restricted to the working directory, temp directory, and . Reads are denied for credential stores (, , , ). Writes to and inside the project are always denied. See security for details. Shell execution Shell commands have a 30-second default timeout and bounded output. Agav auto-detects macOS Seatbelt or Linux Bubblewrap; Docker can be requested as a tool override. streams stdout/stderr, so a large output no longer fails merely by exceeding the old shell buffer. Small results show stdout followed by stderr; oversized results and saved logs use observed arrival order across the two streams. Above 40,000 decoded UTF-8 bytes (or when status/separator formatting crosses that limit), it saves a log and returns a Unicode-safe head/tail preview. The shared registry can additionally truncate results exceeding 2,000 lines. The saved log stops at 16 MiB, but the command continues and its final output tail and exit status remain visible in the preview. A “partial output” notice therefore does not mean the command was stopped or that the log contains its final lines. Nonzero exits, signals, and timeouts remain errors even when stdout exists. Timeout handling attempts to terminate the process tree, escalates termination, and bounds pipe drainage rather than waiting indefinitely for inherited pipes. Storage failure does not rerun a command. Commands are non-interactive: stdin is closed and there is no controlling terminal. Commands that need passwords, SSH prompts, or terminal interaction should be run in your own shell instead. On Unix, native, Seatbelt, and Bubblewrap shell runners own a process group. Failure, cancellation, timeout, buffered-output overflow, and orderly host exit trigger termination, with forced escalation if needed and bounded pipe drainage. Windows uses with forced escalation. This is best-effort cleanup, not rollback: descendants that escape the group and external side effects may remain. Successful background children are not killed merely because the shell leader finishes. Output from children sharing the inherited pipes is collected until the pipes close or the command timeout bounds that wait. A successful leader can still be reported as successful when only pipe drainage reaches the timeout; do not interpret that status as proof that every background job completed. Manage persistent services explicitly. The buffered runners used by some integrations still enforce their own output-buffer limits. Test and agent subprocesses receive cancellation signals but do not inherit the shell runner's process-tree cleanup guarantees. MCP cancellation stops Agav's request wait without killing the shared server; server-side work may continue. Docker cancellation signals the local CLI but does not guarantee daemon/container cleanup. See Security. HTTP responses supports GET (default), POST, PUT, DELETE, and PATCH, with optional headers and body. It streams the response as decoded text, including raw HTML, with a 30-second request timeout. Once started, it does not consume the turn cancellation signal; Esc does not immediately stop that request or undo a POST or other server-side action. Small results include the HTTP status and body unchanged; above 38,000 decoded UTF-8 bytes, a response log and bounded head/tail preview are used. Unlike shell capture, HTTP capture cancels the remaining response when its 16 MiB incoming-byte or decoded-storage limit is exceeded. The notice marks the saved response as partial; the preview tail is from the captured prefix, not necessarily the end of the server's body. Reaching this size limit alone does not turn a successful HTTP status into an error. Non-success HTTP statuses and network/stream-read failures do remain errors, with the captured status/body retained where available. Log-storage failures do not repeat the request or change HTTP success status. The shared text limits and retention rules apply to these results too. Sandbox backends Each sandbox backend has different isolation properties: | Backend | Filesystem writes | Network | Credential dirs | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Seatbelt (macOS) | System directories and home writes denied, with working-directory and standard cache/config carve-outs | Allowed | , , reads denied | | Bubblewrap (Linux) | Read-only root; writable working directory and scratch tmpfs for and standard caches/config | Allowed | , , masked | | Docker | Mounted working directory only | Denied () | Not mounted | When no backend is available, the command runs unsandboxed with secret-like environment variables (, , , …) filtered out. Set to opt out of sandboxing deliberately. Review security before using auto-accept mode.

title: Features
content: Features Agav combines a core toolset with extension points that add reusable knowledge and external capabilities. - Built-in tools cover files, search, shell, background processes, testing, language servers, notebooks, GitHub, web access, plans, and memory. - Background processes start daemon-backed shell commands, keep logs under , and reattach with completion notifications after restart. - Skills package reusable instructions and tool policies, with a built-in marketplace, validation, and automatic improvement. - MCP connects stdio subprocess servers and remote HTTP/SSE endpoints that expose tools, resources, and prompts. - Plugins and subagents add JavaScript tools and parallel task execution. - Agents are specialized sub-agents with scoped tools, credentials, and system prompts. - Agent Marketplace provides community-built agents for cloud platforms, developer workflows, and automation. Tools are chosen by the model based on the task. Read-only operations can run directly; sensitive operations follow the active permission mode and may require confirmation.

title: Model Context Protocol
content: Model Context Protocol Agav connects to MCP servers over two transport families: stdio (local subprocesses communicating through newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout) and remote (HTTP or SSE endpoints). Stdio servers Add to or : Each server supports a command, optional argument list, and optional environment overrides. Restart Agav after changing server configuration. Remote servers (HTTP / SSE) Remote servers connect to an MCP endpoint over the network instead of spawning a local process. Two transport modes are supported: - Streamable HTTP – the current MCP spec transport. Uses a single HTTP endpoint for both requests and server-initiated messages. - Legacy SSE – the older Server-Sent Events transport. Uses one SSE connection for server-to-client messages and a separate HTTP POST endpoint for client-to-server messages. When is omitted, Agav auto-detects: it tries Streamable HTTP first and falls back to Legacy SSE if the server does not support it. Basic configuration is optional when is present — Agav infers the server type automatically. Explicit transport selection If you know which transport the server speaks, pin it with : Remote server config fields | Field | Type | Required | Description | |-------|------|----------|-------------| | | string | yes | HTTP/SSE endpoint URL | | | | no | Explicitly marks the server as remote; inferred when is present | | | or | no | Force a specific transport; omit to auto-detect | | | Record\ | no | Extra headers sent with every request | are sent with every request and are the recommended way to pass authentication tokens. The , , and fields are not used for remote servers. Exposed capabilities - Tools are registered in the main tool pool with their server name prefixed to the tool name and shown in the description. MCP tools are not in the built-in safe list, so they require user confirmation before each call unless you are in mode or the tool is explicitly allowed via . - Resources are summarized in model context and read on demand through . - Prompts become slash commands. Agav requests the rendered prompt from the owning server and submits its messages to the conversation. If one server fails to start, Agav continues without it. Run to see connected server names and counts for discovered resources and prompts. Live refresh When a connected server sends , , or , Agav re-fetches the corresponding catalog from that server and updates the session immediately — no restart needed. This only applies to changes the server advertises at runtime; edits to itself still require a restart. title: Plugins and Subagents
content: Plugins and Subagents Local plugins Agav loads and files from ( on Windows). A module can default-export one tool or export a array. Each tool needs , , , and an async function returning . The argument is an object with the properties defined in . Broken plugin modules are skipped. Plugins execute local JavaScript with the same operating-system access as Agav, so install only code you trust and restart Agav after changes. Parallel subagents The tool delegates a clear, self-contained task with a short UI title. Subagents: - have independent conversation context - inherit the active model, effort, system prompt, steers, permission mode, and available tools - cannot create nested subagents - share confirmations through the main terminal UI - report streaming progress and token usage - allow up to five concurrent tasks While subagents run, the terminal shows a live overview. Use / to select a subagent and to inspect it. Press the cancel key ( by default) to cancel just the focused subagent while inspecting it, or to cancel all running subagents from the overview. See Keybindings for the subagent navigation shortcuts. Tasks whose description indicates file changes attempt to use an isolated Git worktree. Agav applies the resulting changes back to the original checkout and reports a warning if that merge step fails. Read-only tasks use the current working directory directly. Give a subagent all necessary paths, constraints, and expected output because it is instructed to work without follow-up questions. Related - Create a Local Plugin — step-by-step plugin authoring guide - Coordinate Parallel Subagents — patterns for splitting work across subagents

title: Skills
content: Skills Skills are reusable instruction packages that extend Agav with domain-specific procedures. Each skill is a file — YAML front-matter declaring metadata, followed by a Markdown body containing the instructions the LLM follows when the skill is activated. Skills let you encode repeatable workflows (code review, test generation, research) and share them across projects and teams. Loading order Skills are loaded from three tiers. A skill in a later tier with the same slug replaces the earlier definition: | Tier | Location | Override priority | |------|----------|-------------------| | Bundled | Shipped with Agav binary | Lowest | | Global | | Middle | | Project | in the working directory | Highest | When a project skill overrides a bundled or global skill, the override is tracked and shown as in and . If two skills in the same tier share a slug, the second is skipped with a warning. Skills whose slug collides with a built-in command name (e.g. , , ) are also silently skipped. Bundled skills are compiled directly into the binary, so they work even when running from a compiled build where file system paths are unavailable. Bundled skills Agav ships with 21 bundled skills: | Skill | Description | Invocation | |-------|-------------|------------| | | Review code changes for bugs, security issues, and improvements | auto + manual | | | Clean up and analyze CSV/Excel data for non-analysts | auto + manual | | | Multi-source research on a topic with citations | manual | | | Diagnose and fix errors and bugs | auto + manual | | | Generate documentation for code | auto + manual | | | Create, read, edit, and review Word .docx documents | auto + manual | | | Draft emails and replies with the right tone — never sends them | auto + manual | | | Explain code in plain language | auto + manual | | | Clean up a messy folder with a dry-run plan before moving anything | auto + manual | | | Generate a commit message from staged changes | auto + manual | | | Turn raw meeting notes or transcripts into structured minutes | auto + manual | | | Extract text from, merge, split, and fill PDF files | auto + manual | | | Rewrite text to be clear and understandable for any reader | auto + manual | | | Create and edit PowerPoint .pptx presentations | auto + manual | | | Suggest and apply code refactoring | auto + manual | | | Check code for security vulnerabilities | manual | | | Reduce complexity and simplify code | auto + manual | | | Guide for authoring a new agav skill (SKILL.md) | manual | | | Summarize documents, web pages, or pasted text at any depth | auto + manual | | | Generate unit tests for existing code | auto + manual | | | Create, read, and edit Excel .xlsx spreadsheets and CSV files | auto + manual | Using skills Skills can be invoked in two ways depending on their setting: - * — called explicitly as a slash command: - — selected automatically by the LLM when a query matches the skill's triggers - — available both ways Watch a running skill Skills activated through appear in the live subagent overview as Skill: , including when you invoke a skill such as . While the main turn is running, use ↑ / ↓ to select the skill, Enter to inspect it, and Tab to return to the overview. Manual-only () skills such as display their detail panel directly while running; you do not need to press Enter. Before the first activity event, this path shows a “Running skill” spinner. The detail panel shows the task, reasoning summary when the provider emits one, streaming text, and Recent actions (up to 10). Recent actions retain tool inputs, statuses, and available edit diffs across model messages — they do not disappear just because the model starts its next response. This is a recent-activity view, not a complete tool log. The session footer includes skill token usage as provider usage events arrive: ↑ input, ↓ output, ⇢ cache reads, and ⇠ cache writes when present. Completion does not add the skill total a second time. Usage already reported is retained after failure or cancellation; emitted or thrown errors record an unsuccessful trace, but interruption alone does not guarantee that trace status. Unreported provider usage cannot be counted. Tool-activated skill entries share the worker UI but do not support focused Esc cancellation. Return to the overview with Tab, then press Esc to cancel their parent turn. Individual focused cancellation applies only to actual workers. Manual-only slash-command skills currently receive no turn cancellation signal; their progress panel does not make Esc a reliable way to stop them. Permissions still apply A live progress panel does not approve actions. Tool-activated skills inherit the session's permission mode and route sensitive-action approvals to the main terminal. Review the tool input and available diff before approving; continues to block designated file-mutating/destructive tools, but is not a universal read-only or network-side-effect boundary. Manual-only slash-command skills currently run without an interactive confirmation handler. In mode, operations requiring confirmation are refused and fenced shell blocks are skipped rather than approved silently. Use a read-only task in this mode; do not switch to merely to bypass a refusal. See Security for permission modes and Shell blocks for their specific behavior. Automatic dispatch When a user message starts with , Agav immediately activates that skill without planning. This is used internally by the LLM for automatic skill selection. Dynamic context variables Skill bodies support two placeholder variables that are replaced at runtime: - — replaced with the user's arguments, or if none - — replaced with the current working directory Steer integration Active directives from are appended to the skill's system prompt, so user guidance applies even inside skill execution. Installing skills From a local file or directory When pointing to a directory, Agav copies the entire tree (excluding , , , and ). When pointing to a bare SKILL.md file, it copies the file plus sibling asset directories (, , ) if present. Batch install: If the target directory contains no at the root but has subdirectories with files, all subdirectories are installed independently. Failures in one skill don't block others. Size limits: Installations are capped at 200 files and 10 MB total. Exceeding either limit is refused before any files are copied. From a URL Agav normalizes common GitHub URL formats automatically: - → raw content URL - → raw content URL with appended - Bare repo URL → appends If the URL returns an HTML page instead of Markdown, Agav reports a clear error rather than a confusing validation failure. GitHub batch install: If a single URL 404s, Agav checks whether the URL points to a directory containing multiple skill subdirectories and installs all of them. From the marketplace The marketplace opens an interactive TUI with two tabs — Marketplace (browse and install) and Installed (manage what you already have): - Tab to switch between the Marketplace and Installed tabs - ↑↓ to navigate, ←→ to page (5 skills per page) - s to search by name or description - ENTER to install the selected marketplace skill - In the Installed tab, d (or ENTER) toggles a skill between enabled and disabled — this works on bundled skills too - r to refresh the catalog - ESC to exit Already-installed skills show a badge and cannot be reinstalled. In the Installed tab each skill shows its origin and an / state. Removing skills Only global (user-installed) skills can be removed. Bundled skills live inside the binary and project skills belong to the repo, so on one of those reports an error and points you to instead. Removing a global skill also clears any disabled state it had, so reinstalling it later starts enabled again. Restart Agav after installing or removing a skill. Disabling bundled skills Bundled skills are compiled into the binary, so they cannot be removed with or . To turn one off, disable it instead: A disabled skill is excluded from the catalog the model sees, loses its slash command, and can no longer be activated — but it still appears in marked so you can re-enable it. The choice is stored in and survives upgrades. Restart Agav after disabling or enabling a skill. You can also toggle skills from the Installed tab of (press d), or from outside a session with the CLI: Creating a skill A skill is a directory containing a file — YAML front-matter followed by instruction body: Frontmatter fields | Field | Type | Required | Description | |-------|------|----------|-------------| | | string | yes | Unique identifier. Must be lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens (), max 64 chars. | | | string | yes | One-line description, max 1024 chars. | | | string | no | Semver version string. Recommended but not enforced. | | | \| \| | no | How the skill can be triggered. Default: . | | | string[] | no | Whitelist of tools the skill can use. Supports parenthesized qualifiers like . | | | string[] | no | Blacklist of tools removed from the skill's registry. | | | string | no | LLM model override for this skill. | | | string | no | Reasoning effort override. | | | string[] | no | Keywords for search and automatic trigger scoring. | | | string | no | License name or file reference. | | | string | no | Environment requirements (max 500 chars). | | | Record | no | Arbitrary key-value pairs. Agav reads its own extension fields from here as a fallback, so skills authored for other platforms that nest extensions under work the same. | Tool name compatibility The and fields accept both Agav tool names and agentskills.io spec names. Spec names are automatically mapped at runtime: | Spec name | Agav name | |-----------|-----------| | | | | | | | | | | , | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | , | | Shell blocks Skill bodies can contain fenced shell blocks (``deny-writesaskauto-acceptruncommandcmd.exe /c/bin/sh -callowed-toolsdisallowed-toolssubagentactivateskillnamedescriptionversionnameignore all previous instructionsignore all priordisregard previouscurl ... | bashwget ... | basheval()rm -rf /chmod 777sudobase64 | bashallowed-toolsdisallowed-tools.agav/traces.jsonl/skills info ` shows total runs, average tokens per run, and success rate - Trigger phrases — auto-generated positive and negative triggers from the skill's name, description, and tags - Trigger scoring — user queries are scored against triggers to decide automatic activation (multi-word matches score higher, negative triggers reduce the score) - Optimization notes — after 3+ runs, Agav generates suggestions (e.g., "tighten instructions to reduce token usage") - Background improvement** — every 15 turns, triggers, runtime prompts, and optimization notes are refreshed for all skills Related - Author and Evolve a Skill — full walkthrough - Compose Agents, Skills, and Tools — using skills with agents

title: Getting Started
content: Getting Started This path takes you from installation to a safe first change in an existing repository. Before you begin You need: - a terminal - a local Git repository to explore - an API key for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, NVIDIA NIM, or DeepSeek; a Google Cloud service-account JSON file for Vertex AI; or a running Ollama installation The prebuilt Agav release does not require Node.js. Node.js and pnpm are only needed when developing Agav itself. Follow this path 1. Install Agav and verify that the command works. 2. Connect a provider so Agav can use a model. 3. Complete your first task in a real repository, beginning in read-only mode. 4. Configure your project with shared instructions and defaults when you are ready. At the end, you will know how to open the correct workspace, give Agav exact context, review a proposed change, and check what changed. If you are already set up, go directly to the first-task walkthrough.

title: Install Agav
content: Install Agav One command, no Node.js required — Agav ships as a self-contained binary compiled with Bun. Update Agav Agav checks for a newer release on startup and updates itself. Run it by hand at any time: To install a specific release, pass the version explicitly: The automatic check is skipped when is set, when , and when stdout is not a terminal — so scripted runs never block on it. Agav also writes per-project directories inside repositories you've worked in: (cached images) and . Uninstalling never touches those; delete them yourself if you want them gone. Develop Agav from source This route requires Node.js 22 or newer, pnpm 9 or newer, and Git: Use the repository's rather than mixing package managers. title: Configure a Project
content: Configure a Project You can use Agav without project configuration. Add it when a repository has conventions that Agav should follow consistently. Start at the project root Agav treats the current directory as its workspace. Start from the repository root so file suggestions and tools can reach the whole project: paths are relative to this directory and cannot escape it through or symlinks. Add repository instructions Create or at the project root. Agav uses the first non-empty file it finds. Write short, actionable rules that apply across tasks. Put the details of a one-time task in its prompt instead. Save project defaults Project settings live in and override global defaults from ( on Windows). Agav creates or enriches the project file without overwriting values already there. is a global-only setting — set it in or use / at startup. It cannot be set in project configuration to prevent untrusted repositories from silently escalating permissions. MCP servers can be declared in project config so every session in the repository gets the same tools: Do not commit API keys. Use provider environment variables or secure user-level configuration for credentials. See the configuration reference for every field and the full precedence rules. API keys, endpoint overrides, and cannot be set from project config at all — Agav strips them before use — so a committed can never carry a working secret or redirect your requests. This protection comes from that deny-list, not from gitignore: ignoring only guards against committing your own config by accident, and a cloned repo can ship a regardless (even overrides ). See project config restrictions for details. Know what is shared | Item | Scope | | --- | --- | | or | Repository instructions | | | Project defaults (provider, model, , …) | | | Defaults for your user account | | | Reusable skill overrides for this project | | | Project-local agents | | , , and | User-level extensions | | | Per-project memory, auto-saved across sessions | | | Saved interactive sessions | > Windows: paths resolve to (e.g. ). Agav also ships with built-in skills (like , , ) that are always available. Project and user skills can override a built-in skill of the same name. Per-project memory is keyed by a hash of the git root, so Agav remembers context about each repository without storing anything inside the repo itself. See sessions and memory for details. You have completed the beginner path. Continue with daily workflows or use the task finder.

title: Connect a Provider
content: Connect a Provider Agav needs one model provider. The easiest path is: 1. choose one provider 2. set its credential in the same terminal where you will start Agav 3. launch Agav with that provider and model 4. ask one read-only question to confirm it works The default provider is Anthropic — if you run with no flags and no config file, it will try to use Anthropic. If you are not sure which provider to pick, use OpenAI, Anthropic, or Gemini if you already have an API key. Use OpenRouter if you want access to multiple providers behind a single key. Use NVIDIA NIM for NVIDIA-hosted models. Use DeepSeek for DeepSeek's own models. Use Ollama if you want to run locally. Use Vertex AI if you already run on Google Cloud and want Gemini or Claude billed through that project. Fastest path If you already have an OpenAI key, this is the quickest first run: > Windows: Use in Command Prompt or in PowerShell. All commands on this page follow the same pattern. Then ask: OpenAI By default Agav uses the OpenAI Responses API. If you need the Chat Completions API instead (for example behind a proxy that only supports it), pass : Custom base URL (OpenAI-compatible endpoints) Many services speak the OpenAI API without being OpenAI — private gateways, self-hosted deployments, LiteLLM/vLLM servers, or vendors that expose an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Point the provider at one with instead of adding a dedicated provider: Or set it in : The base URL applies only to the provider. When unset, Agav uses OpenAI's default endpoint. Most OpenAI-compatible endpoints implement Chat Completions rather than the Responses API, so pair a custom base URL with if requests fail. If your gateway needs extra HTTP headers — a custom auth header, a tenant selector, or routing metadata — set in . They are sent with every OpenAI-provider request: OpenRouter OpenRouter aggregates multiple model providers behind a single API key. Set the key as an environment variable: Start Agav with OpenRouter: The default model is , which lets OpenRouter choose the best model for each request. You can also specify any model available on OpenRouter: Or set it in : and switch models — see the table below for every provider's mapping. NVIDIA NIM NVIDIA NIM provides access to NVIDIA-hosted models through an OpenAI-compatible API. Set the API key: Start Agav with NVIDIA NIM: The default model is . All models use the prefix: Or set it in : Context window sizes are detected automatically from the NVIDIA API. The API base URL is . DeepSeek DeepSeek provides access to DeepSeek's own models through an OpenAI-compatible API. Set the API key: Start Agav with DeepSeek: The default model is . DeepSeek also offers for faster, lighter responses: Or set it in : Context window sizes are detected automatically from the DeepSeek API. The API base URL is . Anthropic Google Gemini Vertex AI Vertex AI authenticates with a Google Cloud service-account JSON file rather than an API key. Point Agav at the file, then select the provider: Setting the credentials path is what enables the provider; there is no separate on/off flag to keep in sync with it. Agav uses the multi-region endpoint by default — set (for example ) to pin a region instead, which some Claude partner models require. Claude partner models are supported by the same provider and credentials, addressed with the same prefix. Claude models need the versioned ID that Vertex AI exposes, including its suffix: The service account's , , , and optional are read from the JSON file. Agav exchanges the signed credentials for a short-lived OAuth token and refreshes it automatically. Vertex AI's implicit Gemini caching and Claude's ephemeral prompt caching are used automatically when supported. Protect the key file. The service-account JSON holds an unencrypted private key that can act as that service account against your entire Google Cloud project. Unlike the API keys Agav encrypts into , this file is yours to secure: keep it outside the repository, it (on Windows, use file properties to restrict access to your user account), and grant the service account only the role it actually needs. Ollama Start Ollama and make sure at least one model is installed: Agav lists the models available at the default endpoint. You can also select one directly: For a remote Ollama server, set and, when required, . If you prefer host and port separately, Agav also supports and . Agav sizes the context window per model. Set to override that cap when you know your hardware can take more. and models Every provider except Ollama has a preset for (lightweight, quick answers) and (most capable, complex reasoning): | Provider | | | | --- | --- | --- | | Anthropic | | | | OpenAI | | | | OpenRouter | | | | NVIDIA NIM | | | | DeepSeek | | | | Gemini | | | | Vertex AI | | | Ollama has no preset — and fall back to the OpenAI defaults, which won't work on a local Ollama instance. Use to switch models manually instead. Make it stick If you do not want to pass and every time, save defaults in your user config file: - macOS or Linux: - Windows: Example: Agav can also store provider API keys directly in — they are encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, so the file never contains plaintext secrets. Even so, environment variables are the safer choice on shared machines and less likely to end up in version control. Two rules apply to keys stored in : - Global only. Keys must live in , not a project's . Agav strips API keys (and endpoint overrides) from project config before using it, so a key placed in a repository is silently ignored. This protects you from a cloned repo redirecting your credentials. - Environment variables win. If both the environment variable (e.g. ) and the field are set, the environment variable is used. So in your shell always overrides whatever is saved in the file. See Provider credentials in the configuration reference for the full field-to-variable mapping. Verify the connection Start a read-only session in any repository: Replace the provider and model with your choice. Then ask: If Agav reports a missing key, confirm that the matching environment variable is set in the same terminal where you launched Agav. An explicitly selected provider will not silently use a different provider. If the key is set but Agav still cannot connect: - open a fresh terminal and set the variable again - confirm the variable name matches the provider exactly - for OpenRouter, confirm is set and starts with - for NVIDIA NIM, confirm is set and starts with - for Ollama, confirm the server is running and reachable - for remote Ollama, confirm , or plus - for Vertex AI, confirm points at a readable service-account JSON file, and check if a Claude model requires a specific region You can switch providers or models later with . To save defaults, see configuration. Keep cloud API keys out of project configuration and version control. Next: complete your first repository task.

title: Your First Repository Task
content: Your First Repository Task This walkthrough uses prapaa-ai/hello-agav, a tiny Python CLI that greets you and counts its own runs. It is small enough to explore in five minutes and has one obvious thing to improve. You can use the same prompts in your own repository. 1. Open the repository root Start Agav from the directory that contains the whole project. Agav treats that folder as the project root, so it uses it to decide which files it can see, which project settings to load, and which suggestions to offer. 2. Start read-only mode lets Agav inspect the repository while blocking edits. Replace the provider and model if you configured a different one. The interactive session opens with a compact Unicode braille shell logo, , and Stay in the Shell. The name and tagline sit beside the logo on wider terminals and stack below it on narrow ones. The footer shows your provider, model, effort, and session token usage; the logo is a static banner, not a new thinking animation. 3. Ask a focused first question Paste this prompt: Typing opens file suggestions. Choose a path with Up or Down, then press Enter or Tab to attach it. An attachment gives Agav exact context; the question tells it what to do with that context. For this repository, the answer should identify as the entry point and explain how it calls to build the message and to track runs via . 4. Narrow the investigation Follow the broad tour with one concrete path through the code: Focused follow-ups are easier to verify than repeatedly asking for a complete repository summary. If Agav activates a skill or delegates work to subagents, their live progress appears below the transcript. While the main turn is running, use ↑ / ↓ to select a worker, Enter to inspect its task and recent tool actions, and Tab to return to the overview. Manual-only skills show their detail panel directly. See Skills and Coordinate Parallel Subagents for the differences. Markdown links in terminal replies display as , with a bare URL shown only once. Long URLs wrap with the terminal width, and detected URL fragments remain clickable across wrapped lines. Click the visible URL to open it in a browser where one is available. On a remote or headless terminal, copy the URL into your local browser if opening it is unavailable; see Troubleshooting. 5. Make one controlled change Exit Agav, then restart without : Ask for a small change with a clear boundary: The default mode pauses before sensitive actions and shows edit diffs. Check the file path and proposed change before approving. Reject the action and clarify your request if it is broader than expected. 6. Review the result After Agav finishes, review the repository yourself: These commands distinguish Agav's work from changes that already existed. Use before exiting Agav to restore a tracked file edit, or use your normal Git workflow afterward. Tips for longer sessions - Use to reclaim context if the conversation gets long — it summarises history without starting over. - Use to revert the last file edit without leaving Agav. - Resume a past session with instead of starting from scratch. What you learned You now know the core Agav loop: 1. open the repository root 2. begin read-only when learning unfamiliar code 3. attach exact context and ask a specific question 4. narrow the scope before requesting a change 5. review confirmations, diffs, and Git state For scripting and CI, see non-interactive mode — and let you use the same agent from pipelines and automation. Next: add project instructions and defaults, or learn more about files and context.

title: Compose Agents, Skills, and Tools
content: Compose Agents, Skills, and Tools Combine capabilities when one task has reusable rules, quick local checks, and independent investigations. Scenario: review a counter.py change A change to can affect how calls it, what contains, and whether tests still pass. This division keeps responsibilities clear: | Layer | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Skill | Repeatable module-review procedure | | Main prompt | This change, its paths, and the required report | | Direct tools | Small checks needed in the main conversation | | Subagents | Independent downstream investigations | Ask the main agent to reconcile the results before starting an implementation phase. Keep temporary repository paths in the prompt, not in a global skill. Expected result You get one review that covers the counter module and every downstream consumer without making each worker inspect the whole repository. Next: Automate with Loops, Watch, and Schedules.

title: Create an Agent with the Wizard
content: Create an Agent with the Wizard The agent creation wizard lets you build a custom agent in five guided steps — name it, generate a system prompt with your LLM, select built-in native tools, attach MCP servers, and save. Agav writes the manifest for you and registers the agent immediately. This guide walks through creating a agent from scratch, then covers editing existing agents and working with templates. Prerequisites - Agav installed and connected to an LLM provider (needed for automatic system prompt generation) Step 1: Open the Create tab Start Agav and type: Press to switch to the Create tab. This is the "My Agents" hub — it shows your user-created agents, saved templates, and a button at the top. If you haven't created any agents yet, the list will be empty except for the entry. Step 2: Start the wizard Navigate to and press to launch the five-step creation wizard. A progress bar at the top tracks your position through the flow: You can press or at any step to go back to the previous one without losing your input. Step 3: Name and describe the agent The first step asks for two fields: Name and Description. Name — type a short, unique identifier for your agent. Names must be lowercase alphanumeric characters, hyphens, dots, or underscores, with a maximum length of 64 characters. For example: Press or to move to the Description field. Description — write a one-line summary of what the agent does. This appears in the agent list and helps the LLM understand when to route queries to this agent: Press to advance to the next step. Step 4: Review the system prompt Agav sends your name and description to your configured LLM provider and auto-generates a system prompt tailored to the agent's purpose. The prompt streams in real-time inside a bordered preview box. Once generation completes, review the prompt. It typically includes: - A role definition ("You are a GitHub assistant…") - Guidelines for tool usage - Response formatting instructions If the prompt doesn't match what you need, press to regenerate it. You can regenerate as many times as you like — each attempt produces a fresh prompt based on your name and description. When you're satisfied, press to accept the prompt and continue. Step 5: Select native tools (optional) This step lists Agav's built-in tools. Choose only the tools this agent needs: - Press / to navigate the list - Press to toggle a tool on or off The selected names are written to the agent's manifest allowlist. title: Coordinate Parallel Subagents
content: Coordinate Parallel Subagents Use subagents when independent investigations need more context than a few tool calls. Scenario: audit every module in hello-agav The project has separate modules for CLI parsing, greeting logic, and counter persistence. They can be reviewed independently, then compared for consistency. Each assignment includes its files, checks, output, and no-edit constraint because subagents work independently and cannot ask follow-up questions. Review the combined result Use / to select a subagent and to inspect it. Press in the detail view to cancel the focused subagent, or to return to the overview without cancelling. Sensitive confirmations still appear in the main terminal. While a confirmation is visible, denies that tool call rather than cancelling the focused subagent. When all workers finish, ask the main agent to resolve disagreements and remove duplicate findings. Delegate edits only when workers own different files; worktrees reduce interference but do not make overlapping changes safe. Cancellation and time limits From the overview, Esc cancels the parent turn and signals all its subagents to stop. Cancelling from a subagent detail view targets only that worker; its pending confirmations are rejected so it can leave the approval wait. Ctrl+C with no Agav selection exits the application rather than cancelling just one worker. Cancellation can arrive during worktree setup, before the worker starts its agent loop. A cancelled worker does not intentionally merge its partial worktree edits back into the parent. This is not transactional rollback: edits made without a worktree, external actions already performed, or a merge already underway may remain. Review the resulting diff. There is no separate wall-clock timeout for the entire subagent task. Workers inherit the configured iteration limit, and individual tools have their own timeouts. Shell and test subprocesses receive the worker's cancellation signal; custom tools still need to honor it. Cancelling an MCP tool stops Agav's wait, not necessarily the server-side work, and cancelling a Docker command does not guarantee container cleanup. Expected result You receive three bounded audits and one reconciled list of risks across main.py, greeting.py, and counter.py, while the main conversation retains final ownership. Next: Run Tools in Parallel.

title: Run Tools in Parallel
content: Run Tools in Parallel Use parallel tools for short, independent checks that belong in the same conversation. Scenario: understand hello-agav before adding a feature Before adding a new feature, you need to understand three separate parts of the project: - how the CLI parses arguments and calls modules - how the greeting is built - how the run counter works Ask Agav to inspect them together: Agav can run independent reads and searches concurrently, then return the evidence to the same conversation. Keep dependencies in order Do not parallelize steps when one changes what the next step reads. State the order explicitly: Keep overlapping edits and state-changing commands sequential. A successful or invalidates earlier verification. Tests or shell checks in the same parallel tool batch as that edit do not count as post-edit verification, even if their result arrives last. Wait for the edit batch to finish, then run checks in a later batch. Independent checks against the same finished revision can run together. If any check in that batch fails, a passing sibling does not cancel the failure; fix the cause and verify again in a later batch. A result with no recognized passing tests is inconclusive, not proof that the change passed. Passing tests still do not replace any required build, manual run, warning review, or expected-output comparison. See structured test runs for the exact behavior. Tool results remain bounded per result when run concurrently. Parallel reads can still add substantial aggregate context, and large simultaneous captures share the process's temporary-output retention budget. Prefer a focused depth, targeted searches, and file ranges; follow truncation notices when more evidence is needed. Use parallel subagents when each investigation is large enough to need its own context. Expected result You get one concise map of the CLI arguments, greeting format, and counter persistence without waiting for each independent read in sequence. Next: Coordinate Parallel Subagents.

Protect it yourself — see Connect a Provider. Prefer environment variables on shared machines. Project config restrictions To prevent a malicious repository from redirecting API requests or escalating permissions, the following fields are ignored in project configuration and can only be set in global configuration () or via environment variables: - Endpoint overrides: , , , , - API keys: , , , , , , - Permission escalation: These fields are stripped from before it is merged, so a value placed there is silently ignored rather than applied — Agav does not warn about it. This ensures that cloning an untrusted repository cannot silently redirect your credentials to a third-party server or bypass tool confirmations. Set these fields in global config or via environment variables instead. > This is not the same as gitignore. Ignoring in a repository only stops you from accidentally committing your own project config. It does not protect you when you clone someone else's repo: a malicious author can commit a poisoned anyway (for example with , which overrides ), and it arrives on your disk as a tracked file the moment you clone. Your local never applies to it. The deny-list above is the actual defense against that clone-and-run threat, because it strips the dangerous fields at load time regardless of how the file got there. Do not rely on gitignore for credential safety.
